{"learner":"Level: strong Python (classes, dicts, asyncio), but new to Rust and has never used a compiled language.
Goal: go from zero to writing production Rust. These 10 lessons cover the toolchain, types, ownership, borrowing, strings and structs; later lessons cover enums, error handling, traits, async, testing and deployment.
Known strengths: understands shared references in Python.
Known gaps: guessed move semantics correctly but with low confidence; has never seen a borrow checker; has no experience with compile-time workflows.","lessons":[{"id":"compile-and-run","title":"From Source to Executable","objective":"Create, build and run a Rust project with Cargo, and explain what a compile error means.","explain":"Python runs your source through an interpreter, but Rust adds a step first. `rustc` compiles Rust source into a native executable before it runs. A compile error means no executable is produced, so none of the program runs. Running the executable does not require a Rust installation. Cargo drives this: `cargo new` creates a project, and `cargo run` builds and runs it. Every Rust executable starts at `fn main`. Example: `cargo new hello` generates `fn main() { println!("Hello, world!"); }`, and `cargo run` prints Hello, world!","key_facts":["`rustc` compiles Rust source into a native executable before it runs.","A compile error means no executable is produced, so none of the program runs.","Running the executable does not require a Rust installation.","`cargo new` creates a project, and `cargo run` builds and runs it.","Every Rust executable starts at `fn main`."],"fixes":[],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What does `rustc` produce from Rust source?","options":["A native executable","A Python bytecode file","A script for an interpreter","A bundle of source text"],"answer":"A native executable","why":"`rustc` compiles Rust source into a native executable before it runs.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"A program has a compile error on its last line. What happens to the earlier lines?","options":["They run up to that line","None of them run","They run with a warning","Only `fn main` runs"],"answer":"None of them run","why":"A compile error means no executable is produced, so nothing can run.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"You copy a finished executable to a compatible machine. What must that machine have installed from Rust?","options":["The `rustc` compiler","The Cargo tool","The project source files","No Rust installation"],"answer":"No Rust installation","why":"Running the executable does not require a Rust installation.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which command builds a Cargo project and then runs it?","options":["`cargo new`","`cargo start`","`cargo run`","`cargo exec`"],"answer":"`cargo run`","why":"`cargo run` builds and runs the project, while `cargo new` creates one.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"At which function does every Rust executable start?","answer":"`fn main`","accept":["main","fn main","main()","the main function"],"why":"Every Rust executable starts at `fn main`.","tests":4},{"type":"recall","q":"What command creates a new Cargo project named hello?","answer":"`cargo new hello`","accept":["cargo new hello"],"why":"`cargo new` creates a project with the given name.","tests":3}]},{"id":"variables-and-mutability","title":"Variables, mut and Shadowing","objective":"Choose correctly between an immutable variable, a `mut` variable and a shadowing `let`.","explain":"In Python, any name can be rebound at any time. In Rust, `let` creates a variable, and it is immutable by default. Reassigning an immutable variable is a compile error. Adding `mut` allows reassignment and mutation. Shadowing is different: a second `let` with the same name creates a new variable, which may have a different type. Example: `let mut total = 0; total = 5;` compiles, but removing `mut` does not. `let size = "abc"; let size = size.len();` also compiles, because the second `size` is a new variable.","key_facts":["`let` creates a variable, and it is immutable by default.","Reassigning an immutable variable is a compile error.","Adding `mut` allows reassignment and mutation.","A second `let` with the same name creates a new variable, which may have a different type."],"fixes":[],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"What is true of a variable created with plain `let`?","options":["It is immutable by default","It is mutable by default","It is global by default","It is untyped by default"],"answer":"It is immutable by default","why":"`let` creates a variable that is immutable unless you add `mut`.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"What happens with `let x = 1; x = 2;`?","options":["`x` becomes 2 at runtime","`x` silently stays at 1","It is a compile error","It crashes when it runs"],"answer":"It is a compile error","why":"Reassigning an immutable variable is a compile error.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which line lets `count` be reassigned later?","options":["`let count = 0;`","`let mut count = 0;`","`mut count = 0;`","`count = 0;`"],"answer":"`let mut count = 0;`","why":"Adding `mut` to the `let` allows reassignment and mutation.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does `let size = "abc"; let size = size.len();` compile?","options":["The first `size` was implicitly `mut`","The second `let` makes a new variable","`let` converts the old variable's type","Variables have no type until they run"],"answer":"The second `let` makes a new variable","why":"Shadowing creates a new variable, which may have a different type.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"What keyword must you add to `let x = 1;` so that `x` can be reassigned?","answer":"`mut`","accept":["mut","let mut"],"why":"Adding `mut` allows reassignment and mutation.","tests":2},{"type":"recall","q":"What is the term for declaring a new variable with the same name using a second `let`?","answer":"Shadowing","accept":["shadow","variable shadowing"],"why":"A second `let` with the same name shadows the first by creating a new variable.","tests":3}]},{"id":"static-types","title":"Static Types and Numbers","objective":"Read and write type annotations, predict default numeric types, and cast between numeric types.","explain":"Python attaches types to values at runtime. In Rust, every variable has one type, fixed at compile time. The compiler usually infers it, or you can write it, as in `let x: i32 = 5;`. With nothing else to constrain them, integer literals default to `i32` and float literals to `f64`. Rust integers have fixed sizes, unlike Python's arbitrary-precision `int`. Rust does not implicitly convert between numeric types; use `as` to cast. Example: `let a: i32 = 5; let b: i64 = a as i64;` compiles, but `let b: i64 = a;` is a compile error.","key_facts":["Every variable has one type, fixed at compile time.","The compiler usually infers it, or you can write it, as in `let x: i32 = 5;`.","With nothing else to constrain them, integer literals default to `i32` and float literals to `f64`.","Rust integers have fixed sizes, unlike Python's arbitrary-precision `int`.","Rust does not implicitly convert between numeric types; use `as` to cast."],"fixes":[],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"When is a Rust variable's type fixed?","options":["At compile time","At first assignment at runtime","Whenever its value changes","When the program exits"],"answer":"At compile time","why":"Every variable has one type, fixed at compile time.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"With nothing else to constrain them, what are the types of `let a = 7;` and `let b = 7.0;`?","options":["`i64` and `f32`","`i32` and `f64`","`i32` and `f32`","`i64` and `f64`"],"answer":"`i32` and `f64`","why":"Unconstrained integer literals default to `i32` and float literals to `f64`.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"How does Rust's `i32` differ from Python's `int`?","options":["It can only hold even numbers","It is checked only at runtime","It has a fixed size","It grows as values get larger"],"answer":"It has a fixed size","why":"Rust integers have fixed sizes, while Python's `int` is arbitrary-precision.","tests":3},{"type":"mcq","q":"Given `let a: i32 = 5;`, which line compiles?","options":["`let b: i64 = a;`","`let b: i64 = a as i64;`","`let b: i64 = i64 a;`","`let b as i64 = a;`"],"answer":"`let b: i64 = a as i64;`","why":"Rust has no implicit numeric conversion, so you must cast with `as`.","tests":4},{"type":"recall","q":"Write a line that declares `x` with an explicit `i32` type and the value 5.","answer":"`let x: i32 = 5;`","accept":["let x: i32 = 5;","let x: i32 = 5"],"why":"A type annotation goes after the variable name and a colon.","tests":1},{"type":"recall","q":"Which keyword casts one numeric type to another in Rust?","answer":"`as`","accept":["as"],"why":"Rust does not convert numeric types implicitly, so you use `as` to cast.","tests":4}]},{"id":"functions-and-expressions","title":"Functions and Expressions","objective":"Write typed functions that return values and use blocks and `if` as expressions.","explain":"Python type hints are optional, but Rust function parameters must have written types, and a returned type is written after `->`. A block's value is its final expression, written without a semicolon. Adding a semicolon makes it a statement, and the block then evaluates to `()`. `if` is an expression, so `let` can take its value, and its branches must have the same type. Example: `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }` returns the sum. Writing `a + b;` instead is a compile error, because the body then evaluates to `()`, not `i32`.","key_facts":["Function parameters must have written types, and a returned type is written after `->`.","A block's value is its final expression, written without a semicolon.","Adding a semicolon makes it a statement, and the block then evaluates to `()`.","`if` is an expression, so `let` can take its value, and its branches must have the same type."],"fixes":[],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which function signature is valid Rust?","options":["`fn add(a, b) -> i32`","`fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32`","`fn add(a: i32, b: i32): i32`","`fn add(i32 a, i32 b) -> i32`"],"answer":"`fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32`","why":"Parameters must have written types, and the returned type follows `->`.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"What is the value of the block `{ let x = 2; x + 1 }`?","options":["`()`","`2`","`3`","`x`"],"answer":"`3`","why":"A block's value is its final expression, written without a semicolon.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b; }` fail to compile?","options":["The body evaluates to `()`","`a + b` needs a `mut` keyword","The parameters are not declared","Blocks cannot contain arithmetic"],"answer":"The body evaluates to `()`","why":"The semicolon makes it a statement, so the block evaluates to `()` rather than `i32`.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which line compiles?","options":["`let v = if ok { 1 } else { "a" };`","`let v = if ok { 1 } else { 2 };`","`let v = if ok { 1; } else { 2 };`","`let v = if ok { "a" } else { 2 };`"],"answer":"`let v = if ok { 1 } else { 2 };`","why":"`if` is an expression, and its branches must have the same type.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"What does a block evaluate to when its last line ends with a semicolon?","answer":"`()`","accept":["()","unit","the unit value"],"why":"The semicolon makes the last line a statement, so the block evaluates to `()`.","tests":2},{"type":"recall","q":"What symbol comes before a function's returned type?","answer":"`->`","accept":["->","arrow","an arrow"],"why":"A returned type is written after `->`.","tests":0}]},{"id":"ownership-and-moves","title":"Ownership and Moves","objective":"Predict when a `String` moves, which variable owns it, and when it is freed.","explain":"In Python, `b = a` makes two names share one object. Rust is different: every value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory freed. Assigning a `String` to another variable moves ownership, and the old variable can no longer be used. Passing a `String` to a function by value also moves it. Example: `let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a; println!("{a}");` is a compile error because `a` was moved. Using `b` works, and the text is freed once, when `b` goes out of scope.","key_facts":["In Python, `b = a` makes two names share one object.","Every value has exactly one owner.","When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory freed.","Assigning a `String` to another variable moves ownership, and the old variable can no longer be used.","Passing a `String` to a function by value also moves it."],"fixes":["Guessed move semantics correctly but with low confidence, without a rule explaining why a moved variable becomes unusable."],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"After Python's `b = a`, how many objects do the two names refer to?","options":["Two separate objects","One shared object","No object at all","One object per scope"],"answer":"One shared object","why":"In Python, `b = a` makes two names share one object.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"How many owners can a Rust value have at one time?","options":["Exactly one owner","Exactly two owners","As many as needed","None until it is used"],"answer":"Exactly one owner","why":"Every value has exactly one owner.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"When is a `String` dropped and its memory freed?","options":["When a garbage collector next runs","When the program finally exits","When you assign it to a variable","When its owner goes out of scope"],"answer":"When its owner goes out of scope","why":"When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory freed.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"What happens with `let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a; println!("{a}");`?","options":["It prints hi from the shared object","It prints an empty string","It fails to compile because `a` moved","It compiles and then crashes at runtime"],"answer":"It fails to compile because `a` moved","why":"Assignment moved ownership to `b`, so the old variable can no longer be used.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"You call `consume(s)`, where `s` is a `String` and `consume` takes a `String` by value. Can you use `s` afterward, and why?","answer":"No, because passing `s` by value moved it into the function.","accept":["No, it was moved","No, ownership moved to the function","No, s moved into consume"],"why":"Passing a `String` to a function by value also moves it.","tests":4},{"type":"recall","q":"After `let b = a;`, where `a` is a `String`, which variable owns the text?","answer":"`b`","accept":["b","variable b"],"why":"Assigning a `String` to another variable moves ownership to the new variable.","tests":3}]},{"id":"copy-and-clone","title":"Copy and Clone","objective":"Tell when assignment copies rather than moves, and use `.clone()` when you need a second independent `String`.","explain":"Moves are not universal. Types that implement `Copy`, such as `i32`, `f64`, `bool`, and `char`, are copied on assignment, leaving the original usable. `String` is not `Copy` because it owns heap memory, so assignment moves it. Calling `.clone()` on a `String` makes an independent copy of its heap data. Changing a clone does not change the original. Example: `let a = 5; let b = a;` leaves both usable. `let s = String::from("hi"); let mut t = s.clone(); t.push('!');` leaves `s` as hi and `t` as hi!, with both usable.","key_facts":["Types that implement `Copy`, such as `i32`, `f64`, `bool`, and `char`, are copied on assignment, leaving the original usable.","`String` is not `Copy` because it owns heap memory, so assignment moves it.","Calling `.clone()` on a `String` makes an independent copy of its heap data.","Changing a clone does not change the original."],"fixes":["Low confidence about whether assignment moves a value or copies it."],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"After `let a = 5; let b = a;`, which variables are usable?","options":["Only `a`","Only `b`","Both `a` and `b`","Neither one"],"answer":"Both `a` and `b`","why":"`i32` implements `Copy`, so assignment leaves the original usable.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does assigning a `String` move it instead of copying it?","options":["It owns heap memory and is not `Copy`","It is always immutable by default","Its text has no fixed type","It is shared by reference counting"],"answer":"It owns heap memory and is not `Copy`","why":"`String` is not `Copy` because it owns heap memory, so assignment moves it.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which line keeps `s` usable and gives `t` its own text?","options":["`let t = s;`","`let t = s.clone();`","`let t = s as String;`","`let t = copy s;`"],"answer":"`let t = s.clone();`","why":"`.clone()` makes an independent copy of the `String`'s heap data.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"Given `let mut t = s.clone(); t.push('!');`, where `s` holds hi, what does `s` hold?","options":["hi!","An empty string","Nothing, because it moved","hi"],"answer":"hi","why":"Changing a clone does not change the original.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"Name one of the `Copy` types from this lesson.","answer":"`i32`","accept":["i32","f64","bool","char"],"why":"`i32`, `f64`, `bool`, and `char` all implement `Copy`.","tests":0},{"type":"recall","q":"Which method makes an independent copy of a `String`'s heap data?","answer":"`.clone()`","accept":["clone",".clone()","clone()"],"why":"Calling `.clone()` on a `String` copies its heap data.","tests":2}]},{"id":"shared-borrowing","title":"Shared Borrowing and the Borrow Checker","objective":"Pass values by shared reference without moving them, and predict what the borrow checker rejects.","explain":"A Python reference keeps its object alive, but a Rust reference does not. `&value` creates a shared reference, which borrows the value without taking ownership. Many shared references can exist at once, and they are read-only. The borrow checker verifies borrowing rules at compile time. A reference must not outlive the value it points to. Example: `fn size(s: &String) -> usize { s.len() }` lets you call `size(&name)` and still use `name` afterward, because `name` was only borrowed and never moved.","key_facts":["`&value` creates a shared reference, which borrows the value without taking ownership.","Many shared references can exist at once, and they are read-only.","The borrow checker verifies borrowing rules at compile time.","A reference must not outlive the value it points to."],"fixes":["Has never seen a borrow checker, so does not know that it verifies borrowing rules at compile time."],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"After calling `size(&name)`, why is `name` still usable?","options":["`name` was cloned by the call","`name` was only borrowed","`name` implements `Copy`","`name` moved and then came back"],"answer":"`name` was only borrowed","why":"`&value` borrows the value without taking ownership.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which statement about shared references is true?","options":["Only one can exist at a time","They can change the borrowed value","Many can exist, and they are read-only","Each one owns a copy of the value"],"answer":"Many can exist, and they are read-only","why":"Many shared references can exist at once, and they are read-only.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"When does the borrow checker verify borrowing rules?","options":["At compile time","At program startup","During each function call","When memory is freed"],"answer":"At compile time","why":"The borrow checker verifies borrowing rules at compile time.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"A reference `r` points to `x`. `x` goes out of scope, then `r` is used. What happens?","options":["`r` keeps `x` alive, as in Python","`r` becomes an empty value","The program crashes at that line","The code fails to compile"],"answer":"The code fails to compile","why":"A reference must not outlive the value it points to, and this is checked at compile time.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"What symbol creates a shared reference to `name`, as in the call `size(___name)`?","answer":"`&`","accept":["&","ampersand","&name"],"why":"`&value` creates a shared reference.","tests":0},{"type":"recall","q":"Which part of the Rust compiler verifies borrowing rules?","answer":"The borrow checker","accept":["borrow checker","borrowck"],"why":"The borrow checker verifies borrowing rules at compile time.","tests":2}]},{"id":"mutable-borrowing","title":"Mutable Borrowing","objective":"Change a value through `&mut`, and fix code that breaks the rule on mutable and shared references.","explain":"`&mut value` creates a mutable reference, which allows changing the borrowed value. The variable must itself be declared `mut`. At any one time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of shared references. A borrow ends at its last use, not necessarily at the end of its scope. Example: with `let mut s = String::from("hi");`, `let r = &mut s; r.push('!'); println!("{s}");` compiles, because `r` is finished before `s` is read. But `let a = &s; let b = &mut s; println!("{a}");` fails, because `a` is still in use when `b` is created.","key_facts":["`&mut value` creates a mutable reference, which allows changing the borrowed value.","The variable must itself be declared `mut`.","At any one time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of shared references.","A borrow ends at its last use, not necessarily at the end of its scope."],"fixes":["Has never seen a borrow checker, so does not know the rule it enforces on mutable and shared references."],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which reference allows changing the borrowed value?","options":["`&value`","`&mut value`","`mut value&`","`*value&`"],"answer":"`&mut value`","why":"`&mut value` creates a mutable reference, which allows changing the borrowed value.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does `let s = String::from("hi"); let r = &mut s;` fail?","options":["`s` was not declared `mut`","`String` cannot be borrowed","`r` must be declared `mut`","`&mut` needs a `.clone()` call"],"answer":"`s` was not declared `mut`","why":"The variable must itself be declared `mut` before you can mutably borrow it.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which combination of references can be in use at one time?","options":["Two mutable references","One mutable and one shared","Three shared references","Two mutable and one shared"],"answer":"Three shared references","why":"You can have either one mutable reference or any number of shared references.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"Why does `let r = &mut s; r.push('!'); println!("{s}");` compile?","options":["`println!` ignores all borrowing rules","`r` is finished before `s` is read","`push` clones `s` before changing it","`r` takes ownership of a new `String`"],"answer":"`r` is finished before `s` is read","why":"A borrow ends at its last use, not necessarily at the end of its scope.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"State the borrowing rule for mutable and shared references.","answer":"At any one time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of shared references.","accept":["One mutable reference or many shared references, not both","Either one &mut or any number of &"],"why":"The borrow checker enforces this rule at compile time.","tests":2},{"type":"recall","q":"`let a = &s; let b = &mut s; println!("{a}");` fails. Moving the `println!` to which position makes it compile?","answer":"Before `let b = &mut s;`","accept":["before b is created","before the let b line","between the a and b lines"],"why":"A borrow ends at its last use, so `a` is then finished before `b` is created.","tests":3}]},{"id":"string-and-str","title":"String and &str","objective":"Choose between `String` and `&str`, write functions that accept both, and slice text safely by byte range.","explain":"`String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 text buffer. `&str` is a borrowed view of UTF-8 text, called a string slice. A string literal such as `"hi"` is a `&str`. A `&String` can be passed where a `&str` is expected, so functions that only read text should take `&str`. Slice ranges count bytes, not characters, unlike Python's code point indexing. Example: `fn greet(name: &str) { println!("Hi {name}"); }` accepts both `greet("Ada")` and `greet(&owned)`, where `owned` is a `String`. With `owned` holding Ada, `&owned[0..2]` is Ad.","key_facts":["`String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 text buffer.","`&str` is a borrowed view of UTF-8 text, called a string slice.","A string literal such as `"hi"` is a `&str`.","A `&String` can be passed where a `&str` is expected, so functions that only read text should take `&str`.","Slice ranges count bytes, not characters, unlike Python's code point indexing."],"fixes":[],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"Which type owns its text and can grow?","options":["`&str`","`&String`","`String`","`&mut str`"],"answer":"`String`","why":"`String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 text buffer.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"What is a `&str`?","options":["A borrowed view of UTF-8 text","An owned, growable text buffer","A single Unicode character","A copy of a `String`'s heap data"],"answer":"A borrowed view of UTF-8 text","why":"`&str` is a borrowed view of UTF-8 text, called a string slice.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"What type is the literal `"hi"`?","options":["`String`","`&str`","`char`","`&String`"],"answer":"`&str`","why":"A string literal such as `"hi"` is a `&str`.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"What do the numbers in `&owned[0..2]` count?","options":["Characters","Code points","Words","Bytes"],"answer":"Bytes","why":"Slice ranges count bytes, not characters, unlike Python's code point indexing.","tests":4},{"type":"recall","q":"What parameter type should a function use if it only reads text?","answer":"`&str`","accept":["&str","str slice","string slice"],"why":"A `&str` parameter accepts literals and also a `&String`.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"What is the other name for `&str`?","answer":"String slice","accept":["a string slice","str slice"],"why":"`&str` is called a string slice.","tests":1}]},{"id":"structs-and-methods","title":"Structs and Methods","objective":"Translate a simple Python class into a Rust struct with a constructor and methods.","explain":"A Rust `struct` declares named fields with fixed types, so you cannot add attributes at runtime as on a typical Python instance. Methods live in an `impl` block. `&self` borrows read-only, `&mut self` borrows mutably, and `self` takes ownership. Rust has no `__init__`; by convention, an associated function named `new` builds the value, called as `Type::new()`. Example: `struct Counter { n: u32 } impl Counter { fn new() -> Counter { Counter { n: 0 } } fn add(&mut self) { self.n += 1; } }`. Then `let mut c = Counter::new(); c.add();` works.","key_facts":["A Rust `struct` declares named fields with fixed types, so you cannot add attributes at runtime as on a typical Python instance.","Methods live in an `impl` block.","`&self` borrows read-only, `&mut self` borrows mutably, and `self` takes ownership.","Rust has no `__init__`; by convention, an associated function named `new` builds the value, called as `Type::new()`."],"fixes":[],"items":[{"type":"mcq","q":"How can you add a new field to a struct value at runtime?","options":["Assign to the new field name","Call `.clone()` with the field","You cannot add one at runtime","Declare the value with `mut`"],"answer":"You cannot add one at runtime","why":"A `struct` declares its named fields with fixed types up front.","tests":0},{"type":"mcq","q":"Where do a struct's methods live?","options":["Inside the `struct` braces","In an `impl` block","In a `class` block","In `fn main`"],"answer":"In an `impl` block","why":"Methods live in an `impl` block.","tests":1},{"type":"mcq","q":"Which receiver should a method use to change a field without taking ownership?","options":["`self`","`&self`","`mut`","`&mut self`"],"answer":"`&mut self`","why":"`&mut self` borrows mutably, so the method can change fields.","tests":2},{"type":"mcq","q":"How do you normally build a `Counter`, given the conventional constructor?","options":["`Counter::new()`","`Counter.__init__()`","`new Counter()`","`self.new(Counter)`"],"answer":"`Counter::new()`","why":"By convention, an associated function named `new` builds the value, called as `Type::new()`.","tests":3},{"type":"recall","q":"Which method receiver takes ownership of the value?","answer":"`self`","accept":["self"],"why":"`self` takes ownership, while `&self` and `&mut self` only borrow.","tests":2},{"type":"recall","q":"What is the conventional name of the Rust associated function that plays the role of Python's `__init__`?","answer":"`new`","accept":["new","new()","Type::new"],"why":"Rust has no `__init__`, so by convention an associated function named `new` builds the value.","tests":3}]}]}

{"learner":"Level: strong Python (classes, dicts, asyncio), but new to Rust and compiled languages.
Goal: go from zero to writing production Rust.
